A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
128	- P-122 **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position (P-103, "The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word (P-113, "A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
129	- P-126 **Estimates in the project's units.** Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run). "I'm on a max plan. Talk to me in tokens." Costs are given in tokens, never in dollars, and a token count counts writes only, cache writes and new input: "Token counts, always report only writes. Cached reads are de-facto free vis-a-vis writes."
130	- P-127 **Check-ins and stops.** Every overnight or long background run, a batch or any other (a skill rewrite, a redesign worker), is watched by a series of check-ins spaced 45 minutes apart, armed when the run starts, so that the session stays in the prompt cache: hourly ones risk "that this session KV cache is evicted and then the wake-up call pays the full" price, and so would a run's completion arriving after a long silence. The one after a predicted process stop is a single extra. He sends messages at any time (a message during a turn is queued and kills nothing); he does not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; an accidental stop is said so, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished.
131	- P-128 **Where the work lives.** The work runs in the container on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it; transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded`, "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts?", and the lineages are joined at analysis time; the container recovery procedure is a lesson about the remote container (`coordinator/remote-container.md`), not a ledger row. Everything of ours is under `explorations/` ("to remove confusion for any workers"); the inventory note's own move list waits on his reading (parked, `PLAN.md`). Later, a cleaner pass: `main` holds only the changes to the library and the compiler, the whole process record lives on a separate branch, so that a checkout of `main` with full history carries no blobs that are not Fortress; GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches. A post-mortem index points into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that regenerates any verbatim view; the transcript is not restated.
132	- P-129 **The record is public and names models on purpose.** The protocol's rule against model identifiers is the harness's rule for what Claude itself writes and pushes, not a mandate to strip provenance from records that name models on purpose; "We are doing this work in public … there is no need to censor anything"; nothing in a transcript or an index is held back from the tree for that reason. The classifier refused writing this reading into the protocol itself, so it lives here.
133	- P-130 **The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build.** FACTS and POSITIONS are the optimized build, "what is true about the repository snapshot at this moment in time", written timelessly: no dates, no provenance, no account of what changed when or what corrected what; the history files are the debug build, with the full provenance, his quotes at their dates and every earlier text. "I don't want you to be searching with a flashlight in a dark room. I want to give you a map of the territory." A worker or a coordinator appending to FACTS or POSITIONS needs no timestamps; where one is written, or an entry corrects an earlier one, the next consolidation moves that provenance into the history and rewrites the fact or the position without it, at full informational fidelity. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since workers read it and pay the cost. A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, pointing to the report or record that holds the detail, a rung's entry too, since rung entries written at full length, about 14 KB a landed batch, are most of FACTS' growth. The files read at every boot hold a clean current state and do not need edits as the work moves; the narrative of how a landed rung established a fact is history.
134	- P-131 **The delta from the original Fortress is a part of the skill, kept current.** What the revival changed in the original language, each change as the original contradiction and the revival's resolution with its reason, lives in its own part of `fortress-repo`, `references/revival-changes.md` (the name is the writer's to settle), loaded on demand and updated after every batch's landing, so that the next batch reads the fresh version; its `sources.md` traces each entry to the batch landing or the report it comes from. `SKILL.md` is not rewritten for it: it keeps only what does not change from batch to batch and a trigger to read the part. The revival story's part 6 (`explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/revival-story.md`) is its first draft; what `SKILL.md` preloads is settled in the skills rewrite.
135	- P-132 **The order of the work after batch 10.** It was carried out through batch 11, which ran on the rewritten `fortress-repo` and the redesigned workflow. First the skills. `fortress-repo` is rewritten whole by the outline and the seven principles, every part cold-read and fixed. He read and approved `SKILL.md`'s "How a program runs" and the three testing parts; the rest is not held for his reading before batch 11. The three approved parts go through the same pass, and a Fable reviewer compares them with the versions he approved, writing a synthesis of the two where it finds a regression, never a wholesale revert. `coordinator` and `cloud-container` follow later. Then the batch workflow is redesigned: an Opus synthesis of the six batch-10 designs and the measurements of where the batches' tokens went, built into the script with batch 11's manifest, and reviewed by Fable instead of by him. Then batch 11 runs, launched overnight on the standing go, its questions Q1 to Q4 at their recommendations, resumed after the weekly reset if the limit stops it; it is to show the better shape against the wasteful runs before it. The reason for the order: the recent climbing was token-inefficient because the batches re-ran their costly parts, and those causes are what started the skill extraction; a batch run before both are done repeats them.
136	- P-133 **The gap ledger's form.** A row's status cell holds exactly one word of seven: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`; no second status and nothing in brackets; a row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED` and its notes say which half is fixed (D1 of `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md` section 4.5). The rewrite of the ledger is split among many small workers, each with a slice of rows it can hold in context, never one worker over the whole ledger; the duplicate search is a separate step before it, whose groups tell the rewrite which rows to join. The class cell is `kind (area)`, the area one of parser, walk, checker, codegen, runtime, library, prelude, specification, tests, tools; a specification citation gives the file and the section, a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; a row is at most 1,200 characters, the open rows cut to it by the rewrite; the full earlier text of every changed row is in one history file, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md` (D2 to D5 at the proposal's defaults). The rows are sorted into topic sections, the rewrite's topical groups becoming the sections, each row keeping its number; a new row goes into the section its writer names, and row 83 becomes an eight-cell row in its section (D6). `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` owns the ledger's format and is the only way to write it (add with the template checked, note, close, duplicate, check); `facts-extract.sh` stays the one reader of every record, its ledger queries calling `ledger.py`'s parser. D7, numbering rows during parallel batches, is open.
137	- P-134 **The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, and checked against what the workers did.** The skills distil the best practices found by every worker in this repository, for a reader new to it, which every agent is; he judges them with human eyes, and the coordinator helps him write them in the most concise and precise way. Agent shorthand stays where it serves; an internal reference that the record established is explained, since without FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX in context neither he nor an agent can follow it. The skill corrects the assumptions an agent brings from pre-training, so that it forms a correct model of Fortress as a language before it works on the repository that implements it: a "Fortress as a language" section stands in the opening of `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md`, which every agent reads, since nearly every agent writes a test program (`explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md`, `explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md` section D). Where a practice is in question, an archaeology worker checks what the batch workers actually did, as the search for their use of the `fortress` commands did, so that where a better way was found and agents still work around the issue, the skill states the better way. The register is about halfway toward ASD-STE100, Simplified Technical English: one instruction per sentence in the imperative, active voice, short sentences, the condition before the instruction, one word for one thing, no telegraphic or essayist shorthand, and no sentence that tells the reader neither what to do nor a fact needed to do it; without bloating the skills, whose token count matters, a rewrite never longer than what it replaces. Skill text follows ASD-STE100's split: a description of the concepts first, then short procedures, stated positively. He suspects the essayist register came into the skills from FACTS and POSITIONS, written in it by earlier models. Building happens in one area at a time (the interpreter, the compiled path, the library, the specification), which is why the parts are split by area; the skill says so in those terms. `SKILL.md` holds the concepts and the trigger to switch modes; the exploring procedure is a part loaded when the trigger fires. Knowledge that daily work needs stands in the part an agent loads when it needs it; a note stays named in a skill only with a trigger, when to open it, and a narrow way to read it. The record (FACTS, POSITIONS, the ledger, INDEX and the notes) is the project's memory, kept in the repository because a session can move to another container; `fortress-repo` defines it near its top, with its files, and the `coordinator` skill picks each worker's slice of it, so that the dependency runs one way and a worker never needs the `coordinator` skill. How a Claude Code session behaves (long commands, waits, interrupts, the permission check) belongs in `fortress-repo`, which every worker has loaded, not in a skill of its own; what only the coordinator needs of it goes to `coordinator`. The checker count and the distance are the ladder's metrics: the workflow's prompts say how to run them and the `coordinator` skill names them; `fortress-repo` holds nothing of them. `fortress-repo` carries no batch structure, on purpose: which roles exist, who builds, checks, runs the gate, commits and pushes to `main` are set by whoever writes the workflow or the brief, so that agents designing a workflow from the skill are not steered toward ours; the skill says how to do each thing, and the brief says which an agent does. The role split may later be written as behaviours a batch's instructions point to, in a skill of its own. An agent acts on its brief alone: the skill names no other authority over what it commits or pushes, and no rule an agent cannot act on (it cannot ask him). A worker works with three things, its brief, the record and the original tree, in one of two modes: building, where it stands on the record and carries out its mission, and exploring, where it has met something the record does not settle (a gap, two of the team's sources in conflict, new evidence against a decision), gathers evidence in the record first and then in the original tree, adds what it found to the record and returns to building. Where the team's sources disagree, the later one wins, the specification included. A worker never settles such a conflict itself, and never revises the specification to a later source on its own reading: the conflict is surfaced, and the curator rules after research by the nine steps; a decision on record is carried out, and questioned only on evidence the decision did not use. A conflict between the text and an implementation that no decision settles gets a ledger row and a test of the current behaviour; an `XXX` test belongs to repair work, where the current behaviour is tolerated for a time on purpose and the test is promoted once the fix is in. What a worker builds on while its question waits for him is left unsaid: it is case by case, and a reversible choice takes the path of least resistance without a rule. An agent takes the tree it starts from as green, starts with its own failing test, reuses only what its brief cites or its own work ran, and runs more only where its edit reaches; test first applies to an edit of source code. A point a brief wants reviewed is a "point to report", never a "stop", which reads as a condition that stops the worker. A skill's parts are written by the seven writing principles (`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`), which he has read and judged safe to apply to every rewrite: the writer applies them to a whole part at once, and he then reads it, not comment by comment. The earlier lenses note and the review-style profile are not a writer's brief. Before he reads a rewritten part, a cold reader given only the skill reads it as the workers who use it would, flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, the undefined terms and the gotchas; the coordinator reviews the findings, the writer fixes them with his comments so far, and only then does he read it. A comment on the review page marks a problem area, not a sentence to patch: the fix is made at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind. The skills are rewritten in place, git holding the earlier text. One writer does the writing, briefed by the coordinator, every comment fix on the page among its tasks, made from the coordinator's brief of his comment instead of the coordinator interpreting his words: it edits the skill files and commits them, and the coordinator keeps the review page in step, so that the writer's context holds only the writing. The writer is a headless Claude session (`explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`), since such a session keeps its prompt cache for an hour, as the coordinating session does, while an Agent-tool subagent keeps it for five minutes and so writes its whole context again when the curator's next comment comes later than that; the cache's one-hour writes cost more and are worth it. It is resumed for each writing task, and started fresh with only its standing brief when its history no longer serves, as after a large pass or the coordinator's compaction. Its standing order: ASD-STE100 at least halfway, terms defined first and then used, concise procedures, positive phrasing; and it does not take the register of what it reads, since FACTS, POSITIONS and many notes were written by earlier models in agent shorthand that the curator cannot follow cold, and the coordinator, which carries them in context, keeps drifting into it. A writer's minor decisions not taken are settled by the coordinator from the record, as his executive assistant, and not put to him; he is asked only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. A position's bold title here is the record's handle, not his words, and is never quoted to him as his. A glossary of terms, in a skill or on a page, is written as a dictionary is: each term and the noun phrase that opens its definition with no article ("revival", not "the revival").
138	- P-135 **The coordinator rewrite's goals.** The `coordinator` skill is rewritten by a heavier process than `fortress-repo`'s, since the coordinator acts in several roles that work well and must not be lost to an ill-considered change. Its goals: one home for how the coordinator works, the protocol retired and its rules that bind workers moved to `fortress-repo`; every kind of record with one home and a stated purpose, the informal homes (the handover's first section, the held list, PLAN's old rule sections, the boot note's standing lines) retired or folded in, and the skill saying plainly what goes where; a lighter boot that keeps his awareness (the coordinator knows the project without him, never re-asks a decision, never sends a worker to measure again what is on record), the open question being FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX (their form, a grouping by topic, what they repeat of each other, what is always loaded and what is looked up), settled on evidence and a trial boot, not assumed; FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving workers' briefs; no role lost (executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst); the `fortress-repo` writing standard. The skill is tiered: a core always loaded, and sections loaded when the coordinator switches into a mode of work that is not needed all the time (running and reviewing a batch, process engineering, a post-mortem, among others), as the workers' skill separates building from exploring; the coordinator's modes are identified and described first. The batch workflow is in scope, since it is improved whenever it shows a problem. `cloud-container` follows by the `fortress-repo` method. The rewrite rests on the frontier model's own habits, not on a system designed around them: "I don't want a system of hundreds little rules with potentially contradicting dos and don'ts." The skill guides lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to him in each situation, and the record is organized as the model organizes knowledge by itself: "Organization of the knowledge base should reflect the model's second nature, never fight it", which he names the rewrite's highest risk. So the natural baseline of the current models, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, is established before the design, and the design starts from what this project's environment adds to it: his review on a phone, dictation by speech to text, holding the open items of a long dictated message (preventing the wall-of-text spiral and recovering from it), and keeping a large body of project knowledge in order. The map also gives where each record home came from and which model made it. The map of the shape the rewrite starts from is `coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md`. The skill is written from scratch by an Opus writer, from the sort of the rules against the baseline (what is kept, and the facts stated instead of rules), the map's problems to design against, and the writing principles; the writer does not read the existing skill, which is not refactored. A check against the sort's list after the draft shows whether anything kept was lost, and then the cold read follows as usual. A rule is kept when the failure it guards against is on record; the interview's self-report decides no drop, since the two disagree exactly on the rules that matter (the clock, closed decisions), and the interview showed only the record's default shape, a short current-state file with decisions and history apart, which is kept without instruction. The two sorts carry the map's handles, not the rule texts, and are not what he or the writer judges a rule by.
139	- P-136 **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.
140	
141	## How he wants to be spoken to
142	
143	- P-140 **The register.** "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations; replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. A wall of text is one he cannot absorb; the failure mode "is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." Label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication). The coordinator's replies take the register set for the skills, ASD-STE100 about halfway (the entry P-134, "The skills are written for a reader new to the repository ..."): one instruction per sentence, active voice, short sentences, one word for one thing, no shorthand; it had a good effect on the clarity and the tone of the workers' reports. Phrases that read as a flourish are out: a coda tacked on after a semicolon ("by his decision", "the way through is his", "a session cannot wake itself otherwise"); a sentence ends where its point ends.
144	- P-141 **Asks and decisions.** Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs ("What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? ... this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding"); one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation, and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
145	- P-142 **Ownership.** "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival": every re-approval row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
146	- P-143 **The coordinator's standing goal** is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected. This came out of a compaction that left him "out of control, unaware of crucial details" while the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts". The coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".
147	- P-144 **While a batch runs**, no progress reports on it until it lands. He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time. The harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently, declined without a word while work is in flight, and never mentioned to him. He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; "is anything in flight" is answered from the tree, not from the UI.
148	- P-145 **Format.** "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list": no tables in chat, lists. "write the numbers just as K or M. I'm fine as a programmer understanding what a kilo is": never spelled-out thousands and millions, and a numbers message carries few numbers, each with its meaning. Time is spoken from the clock or the record (when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires), never from feel, "yesterday", "this morning", "last night", when the events were minutes or hours apart (protocol § 3). On his phone he reads a page while iOS's Speak reads it aloud at a fast rate, so every page for him has a Select button beside each larger section's heading that selects that section's text for Speak; a section's evidence and references are gathered at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points, and the Select button leaves them out, so that listening never runs through citations.

<!-- What Pavol has decided, holds or already knows, as it stands now: each position in plain words, what we do and why, under a bold title that is its handle; a quote only where his words are the position itself. Timeless: no dates, no provenance, no account of how a position was reached. That record is `POSITIONS-history.md`, where every earlier text of every entry stands verbatim with what became of it. A position he has replaced is gone from here and the later one stands; a decision not yet built keeps the detail the coming work needs. A worker or a coordinator may add an entry with a date or a quote in it; the next consolidation compiles that out into the history and leaves the position. Standing directives about how we work are in `explorations/protocol.md`, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. Read whole at session start, so that none of it is re-asked or re-explained. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast.** The judge is `Specification/`, the Working Draft of February 2011 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it (P-25). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states the revival's changes (P-95). The floor to measure against is a pure-Java microGPT, not yet written (PLAN phase 6).
- P-8 **Where the designers left no word, he decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** He accepts the language's unfinished corners rather than stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the type papers or the library, and takes the designers to have known more than he does. So a review checks his decisions against their intent, for errors of commission and of omission; its items are decisions in this file. Detail: `reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md`, "In short".
- P-9 **The search is for microGPT's most readable expression.** In his words, "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." The two sources are Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation, with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms. The flat program in Hsu's style, C4, fell short, so polishing happens in the vocabulary, the operations the model is written in. C4 is the APL program's target form. Its hyperparameters are tuple bindings, the form an APL strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form of those lines is set aside.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its remaining ground, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, is not pursued.** Its sub-language expands APL to Fortress code over native arrays, and its APL microGPT program stays in the walk check (P-30).
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless he asks.** Fortify's mathematical rendering bakes one view of a computation into the syntax, though the same mathematics can be written many ways. APL's one glyph for each transformation does that better. It is presentation only, off the path, and no argument for Fortress.
- P-12 **The type checker on interpreter programs comes after the switch-over.** He wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs, and sees it as low-hanging fruit. Today it checks only against the compiler's prelude (F-9). It comes once walk also takes the static coercions that the checker inserts (P-59).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-16 **He reads the project's end as the price of doing no work on performance.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into its third phase in 2006, and the project went on at Sun Labs until 2012. The team worked on syntax, and the compiler that was to make the mathematical types fast never came; the funding was cut for good reason.
- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main cost on microGPT's array kernels (F-11). Boxing is measured on microGPT-shaped kernels, not on a scalar loop with literals and a `:=` accumulator, which microGPT never runs. The storage is P-84's decision; unboxed arithmetic is PLAN phase 6 (P-33).
- P-18 **He is coming round to Hsu's view that language paradigms are accidental complexity.**
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted on its history.** The files that still say so wait for the lineage cleanup (PLAN, "Off the path, parked"), which `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists. His plan to make the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch `main` is not carried out (F-165). The third-party Java 9 port gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." (moves to the fortress-repo skill's records part)

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished 2012 restart (F-166) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, it is their latest intent, which the goal is to finish. It covers the exclusion rule, as instantiation exclusion in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, and `Bottom`, which no program can write.
- P-26 **The type group's late positions outweigh the specification's early text where they conflict.** The early text was a wish. The type group then made the language run, for performance and with specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. So their later word wins: the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiler prelude's tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 (P-43), Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper. The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side. ### How we work

- P-104 **Nothing is built or run twice on the same code.** "We don't want to re be rebuilding stuff that doesn't need to be rebuilt." The design, agreed with him and built into the batch script: the old code, the batch's base, is built once per batch, by the coordinator, before the launch, in a worktree nobody compiles or runs in (the script's `args.baseBuild`); "We just mechanically take the latest build and share it between each rung from the same baseline": every rung worktree is seeded from that one build in seconds (`coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean; the worker builds only what its own edit changed; the skeptic builds nothing to check, "very smart skeptics that just like reuse everything that was built during the rank phase as much as possible and just do their independent checks": it reads test-first from the worker's transcript, runs its own small programs on the new code with the rung's build and on the old code from the batch's one base build, through `coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder under the rung's worktree, so that no two agents compile into one cache. What the skeptic finds it fixes itself, test first, and a judge rules on a fix only where it is contested (P-118, "The judge's rulings."), his saving of the refusal chain; the fix is a new code state, built once and its suite run once, with no second skeptic after it and a repair round only on a judge's word. Its goals: one home for how the coordinator works, the protocol retired and its rules that bind workers moved to `fortress-repo`; every kind of record with one home and a stated purpose, the informal homes (the handover's first section, the held list, PLAN's old rule sections, the boot note's standing lines) retired or folded in, and the skill saying plainly what goes where; a lighter boot that keeps his awareness (the coordinator knows the project without him, never re-asks a decision, never sends a worker to measure again what is on record), the open question being FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX (their form, a grouping by topic, what they repeat of each other, what is always loaded and what is looked up), settled on evidence and a trial boot, not assumed; FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving workers' briefs; no role lost (executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst); the `fortress-repo` writing standard. The skill is tiered: a core always loaded, and sections loaded when the coordinator switches into a mode of work that is not needed all the time (running and reviewing a batch, process engineering, a post-mortem, among others), as the workers' skill separates building from exploring; the coordinator's modes are identified and described first. The batch workflow is in scope, since it is improved whenever it shows a problem. `cloud-container` follows by the `fortress-repo` method. The rewrite rests on the frontier model's own habits, not on a system designed around them: "I don't want a system of hundreds little rules with potentially contradicting dos and don'ts." The skill guides lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to him in each situation, and the record is organized as the model organizes knowledge by itself: "Organization of the knowledge base should reflect the model's second nature, never fight it", which he names the rewrite's highest risk. So the natural baseline of the current models, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, is established before the design, and the design starts from what this project's environment adds to it: his review on a phone, dictation by speech to text, holding the open items of a long dictated message (preventing the wall-of-text spiral and recovering from it), and keeping a large body of project knowledge in order. The map also gives where each record home came from and which model made it. The map of the shape the rewrite starts from is `coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md`. The skill is written from scratch by an Opus writer, from the sort of the rules against the baseline (what is kept, and the facts stated instead of rules), the map's problems to design against, and the writing principles; the writer does not read the existing skill, which is not refactored. A check against the sort's list after the draft shows whether anything kept was lost, and then the cold read follows as usual. A rule is kept when the failure it guards against is on record; the interview's self-report decides no drop, since the two disagree exactly on the rules that matter (the clock, closed decisions), and the interview showed only the record's default shape, a short current-state file with decisions and history apart, which is kept without instruction. The two sorts carry the map's handles, not the rule texts, and are not what he or the writer judges a rule by.
- P-136 **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.

## How he wants to be spoken to

- P-140 **The register.** "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations; replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. A wall of text is one he cannot absorb; the failure mode "is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." Label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication). The coordinator's replies take the register set for the skills, ASD-STE100 about halfway (the entry P-134, "The skills are written for a reader new to the repository ..."): one instruction per sentence, active voice, short sentences, one word for one thing, no shorthand; it had a good effect on the clarity and the tone of the workers' reports. Phrases that read as a flourish are out: a coda tacked on after a semicolon ("by his decision", "the way through is his", "a session cannot wake itself otherwise"); a sentence ends where its point ends.
- P-141 **Asks and decisions.** Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs ("What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? ... this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding"); one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation, and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
- P-142 **Ownership.** "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival": every re-approval row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
- P-143 **The coordinator's standing goal** is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected. This came out of a compaction that left him "out of control, unaware of crucial details" while the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts". The coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".
- P-144 **While a batch runs**, no progress reports on it until it lands. He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time. The harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently, declined without a word while work is in flight, and never mentioned to him. He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; "is anything in flight" is answered from the tree, not from the UI.
- P-145 **Format.** "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list": no tables in chat, lists. "write the numbers just as K or M. I'm fine as a programmer understanding what a kilo is": never spelled-out thousands and millions, and a numbers message carries few numbers, each with its meaning. Time is spoken from the clock or the record (when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires), never from feel, "yesterday", "this morning", "last night", when the events were minutes or hours apart (protocol § 3). On his phone he reads a page while iOS's Speak reads it aloud at a fast rate, so every page for him has a Select button beside each larger section's heading that selects that section's text for Speak; a section's evidence and references are gathered at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points, and the Select button leaves them out, so that listening never runs through citations.

I've applied the fixes from all three checks and committed them; nothing is pushed. The core is 14,984 bytes and the whole skill 40,987, so both limits hold. To stay under them I cut repeated text, and the one-line reason after a few rules, but no rule.

**Commit:** `f6bc1aa75` "coordinator skill: the fixes of the kept-list check, the cold read and the trial boot".

**Sizes, before → after**

| File | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `SKILL.md` | 14,198 | 14,984 |
| `delegating.md` | 7,400 | 6,523 |
| `batch.md` | 5,583 | 6,861 |
| `record.md` | 6,298 | 5,828 |
| `road.md` | 1,833 | 1,892 |
| `skill-rewrite.md` | 2,948 | 3,124 |
| `analysis.md` | 2,131 | 1,775 |

**1. The kept-list check**
- **Losses L1 to L6** are restored:
  - L1: a result goes in the turn's final text.
  - L2: a probe or an Opus worker is launched without asking.
  - L3: `FACTS.md` is read in pages.
  - L4 and L5 are in `skill-rewrite.md`: check a practice against what the workers actually did, and keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`.
  - L6: a page's glossary is written as a dictionary.
- **L7** is left for you to move to PLAN.
- **Meaning changes M1, M2 and M4 to M10** are restored as `kept.md` proposed. M2 uses your wording: the curator is not told about edits to the record, and "noted" is only the reply to a request to record words. M9 now sits in `road.md` with the re-approval rows.
- **M3** stays as I wrote it.
- I also fixed four of the minor points, because each fix was cheap: m1, m3, m4 and m7. m2, m5 and m6 are covered below.

**2. The cold read**
- **"Stop" now has four names:**
  - interrupt: the stop of a turn;
  - process stop: the end of the session's process;
  - hold: a decision that the work waits on;
  - reserved point: a point that a batch record keeps for the curator.
- **New terms in the core:** land, model program, fork, cross-area question, bare go, standing go, review list, tokens written.

name: coordinator
description: "Use this skill in the Fortress revival's coordinating session whenever the curator (who decides what is committed and what agents do) is directing you, waiting on you, or setting how the conversation goes. Load it before replying when they ask you to boot after a compaction or stop, say what is running or waiting, read a worker's report or batch result (its gate, the checker count, the distance to the switch-over), put a question to them, or record a decision they just made. Load it too when they say they will review your turns one by one, ask you to hold or restate something, keep quiet during a batch, or change your register or format. **record**

**entry**

**land**

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured.

**fork**
: Design question with more than one way forward.

**cross-area question**
: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.

**ask**

**hold**

**review list**
: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: items for the curator's later review.

**interrupt**

**process stop**

## The standing goal

You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.

- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
- Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.

## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision on record;
- changes a line of the model program;
- answers a cross-area question;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.

- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.

## The facts of this environment

- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
- The git-check hook asks for a commit after every turn. Its reminders are advisory.
- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.

- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.

**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:

1. The question, in one line.
2. The context, in short bullets. Where the subject is new, start with a refresher: why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it.
3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs.
4. What a yes commits the curator to, and what a no costs.
5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.

Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.

**Quiet times.**

- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree.
- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end or a hold. It reaches the phone only outside the app.

**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. Your default, an answer to each point as it comes, buries the curator in text.

- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing.
- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.

**Pages.**

- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.

## The record: what goes where

Under `explorations/coordinator/`:

- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages.
- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
- `review-queue.md`: the review lists, sorted by theme.

Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.

- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.
- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, read these in order:

1. `CLAUDE.md`, then this file.
2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: the Read tool's page holds 25K tokens, and the file is larger.
3. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
5. The boot note, then the held list.
6. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
7. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.

- Read nothing else. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
- After each process stop, tell the curator in one line that the git-check hook is back on. Only the curator can turn it off again, by switching the session to manual mode (`cloud-container`, its hooks part).

## The parts

- `references/delegating.md`: before you brief, launch, watch or resume any worker.
- `references/batch.md`: for a batch, from its preparation to its review.
- `references/road.md`: for PLAN's order, a fork, or idle time.
- `references/record.md`: before you edit FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX or a history file.
- `references/skill-rewrite.md`: when a skill is to change.
- `references/analysis.md`: to measure the work, or find out what happened.
- `references/sources.md`: each rule's source, for maintenance only.

# The skill writer's standing brief

You are the writer for the project skills of the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. The skills are under `.claude/skills/`.

The coordinating session briefs you. It resumes this session for each writing task. Keep this brief in mind after a task ends. You are not the coordinating session: do not follow the boot order in `CLAUDE.md`, and do not read `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` or `INDEX.md` unless a task names an entry.

The curator is the person who directs this restoration. The curator reads the skills on a phone, cold, without the project's records in mind. Every agent that works in the repository reads them in the same way.

# Your standing order

These rules hold for every task.

## 1. Write in ASD-STE100, at least halfway

ASD-STE100 is Simplified Technical English. It has two kinds of text, and you need both:

- **Descriptive text** says what a thing is and how it works. Give the most important information first. Write one topic in each paragraph. Keep each sentence to 25 words or fewer.
- **Procedural text** gives steps. Write one instruction in each sentence. Put the condition first: "If X, do Y." Use the imperative. Keep each sentence to 20 words or fewer.

Describe first, then give the procedure. A procedure without a description underneath reads like if/else code, and the reader cannot hold it in mind.

More rules:

- Define a term before you use it. After that, use the same word for the same thing every time. Do not use two words for one thing, or one word for two things.
- Define a term in the skill's glossary only if it recurs with one meaning. Elsewhere, write plain words.
- Say what to do. Use "do not" only where no positive instruction says the same thing.
- Do not fold a list into a sentence. Use a vertical list.
- Keep the small words: "the", "a", "that". Do not write in telegraphic shorthand.
- Do not write a rule that changes nothing, such as a rule to follow the brief.
- A rewrite of existing text is never longer than the text it replaces. New content that a task asks for is the exception.

Example. Bad: "Name the way that changes nothing." Good: "Tell which solution keeps the current behaviour."

## 2. The glossary form

A skill's terms open the skill, in `SKILL.md`, as a definition list with no heading. Each term is bold on its own line. The definition follows on the next line, after ": ". It opens with a noun phrase. Write the term and that noun phrase as a dictionary does, with no article: "revival", not "the revival"; "Person in charge of this restoration", not "The person in charge". The curator chose this form. `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` is the model.

## 3. Do not take the register of what you read

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, the batch records and many notes were written by earlier models. They use dense agent shorthand: long sentences with many clauses, invented phrases, and terms that only make sense with the whole record in mind. Read them for their content only. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts or resumes the skill writer: a headless Claude session that edits the
# project skills. A headless session writes its prompt cache with the one-hour
# life, where an Agent-tool subagent gets five minutes, so a writer resumed
# within the hour reads its context from the cache.
#
# Usage:
#   skill-writer.sh new <task-file>     a fresh writer: the standing brief
#                                       (../skill-writer-brief.md), then the task
#   skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>  the task, sent to the current writer
#
# The session id and each task's JSON output are kept under the repository's
# tmp/skill-writer/, which is ignored. The script prints the writer's report,
# its session id and the tokens the task wrote to the cache.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.." && pwd)
state="$repo/tmp/skill-writer"
mkdir -p "$state"
mode=${1:?new or resume}
task=$(cd "$(dirname "${2:?task file}")" && pwd)/$(basename "$2")
tools=(Read Edit Write Glob Grep
       "Bash(git add:*)" "Bash(git commit:*)" "Bash(git diff:*)" "Bash(git log:*)"
       "Bash(git status:*)" "Bash(git show:*)" "Bash(git grep:*)" "Bash(wc:*)"
       "Bash(explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh:*)"
       "Bash(python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py:*)")
out="$state/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-$mode.json"
cd "$repo"
case $mode in
  new)
    id=$(python3 -c 'import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())')
    echo "$id" > "$state/session"
    { cat explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md
      printf '\n# Your first task\n\n'
      cat "$task"; } |
      claude -p --model opus --session-id "$id" --permission-mode acceptEdits \
        --allowedTools "${tools[@]}" --output-format json > "$out" ;;
  resume)
    id=$(cat "$state/session")
    claude -p --model opus --resume "$id" --permission-mode acceptEdits \
      --allowedTools "${tools[@]}" --output-format json < "$task" > "$out" ;;
  *) echo "usage: $0 new|resume <task-file>" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
python3 - "$out" <<'EOF'
import json, sys
d = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
u = d.get('usage') or {}
print(d.get('result', ''))
print('---')
print('session', d.get('session_id'), 'turns', d.get('num_turns'),
      'cache writes', u.get('cache_creation_input_tokens', 0) + u.get('input_tokens', 0),

This task has two parts: a few edits to `fortress-repo`, then `cloud-container` rewritten whole. The `coordinator` skill was rewritten tonight (`.claude/skills/coordinator/`); read its `SKILL.md` once, so that you know what it already holds and which parts of the other two skills it names ("`cloud-container`, its stops part", "its hooks part", "`fortress-repo`'s committing part", "its session part"). Keep those part names.

The curator approved tonight's run without reading in between (17:13 UTC, 2026-10-13): "you have my approval to run overnight to the consolidated record, to this coordinator skill extraction, as well as the container skill using the processes we've established". His goal for the night (17:23 UTC): "We have saved a significant amount of space, but not lost any reasoning capabilities from the status quo." For the skills this means: every rule that leaves the record lands in a skill, and no skill grows by more than the new rules it receives.

Read every rule text below at commit `f6bc1aa75` (`git show f6bc1aa75:explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, and the same for `POSITIONS.md`), since a worker is removing the moved entries from the files tonight. An entry is a line that starts with `- F-n` or `- P-n`; `facts-extract.sh 'F-197'` prints one from the working tree while it is still there.

`record-growth.png`, three panels on one time axis, a vertical line at each batch's landing:

- The ledger went from 83 rows (39.6K characters, 09-09) to 638 rows (1.25M) by batch 10 on 10-03. Its first 309 rows (326K) came before the first climb; to batch 10 the 20 landings, with their run windows, added 16 rows and 46K characters each on average.

- Batches 11, 12 and 13 landed on 10-09 (04:05, 14:39 and 23:03 UTC), after 5.5 days with no batch (10-03 10:58 to 10-08 23:42). From batch 10's landing to batch 13's the ledger gained 55 rows and 56K characters (the growth of its commits, not the cuts of the closes), 18 rows and 19K for each landin

# The coordinator's boot

At session start and after every compaction, the coordinating session reads these in order. The `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`, "The boot", gives this order and the rules around it.

1. `CLAUDE.md`, then the `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`.
2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. `FACTS.md` is read in pages.
3. `check-index.sh`, run, and an INDEX line added for each note that it reports.
4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
5. `BOOT.md`, the boot note, then `HELD.md`, the held list.
6. `git log --oneline -15`.
7. If the boot note says that a batch runs: the skill's `references/batch.md`, and what its "While it runs" names.

How the record is kept (FACTS, POSITIONS, their history files, INDEX and the gap ledger) is the skill's record part, `references/record.md`.

## 6. The process stopped in the gate

You are the coordinator. The platform's cap stopped the session's process during climb batch 14's run and restarted it in resume mode a minute later. At the stop, the run stood so: every rung and skeptic had returned; the gather had returned and its commits are on `main`; the gate was in its suites, with the distance stage it had started in the background still running; the commit stage had not begun. Since the launch you had edited the workflow script once: one sentence added to the commit stage's prompt. The run's journal is on disk. The entry you have at hand:

{FACTS 201}

Decide what you do, in what order, and what you do not do. Say what you check on disk first; how you bring the run back and with what; which agents run again and which do not; what you do about the script edit; and what the stopped gate may have left behind that the resumed one meets.

---

## 6. The process stopped in the gate

**The right answer.** First read what is on disk: the run's journal, `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/journal.jsonl` (`coordinator/tools/journal-text.py` reads it), which shows a `result` line for every rung, skeptic and the gather and none for the gate; `git status` and `git log` on `main` (the gather's commits are there); and the processes still alive: the distance stage's JVM and any `ant` suite the gate started in the background survive the restart, so they are found with `ps` and either left to finish or stopped before the resumed gate starts its own, sinc

**Facts it rests on, and where each lives.**

| Fact | Old FACTS 201 | New FACTS 201 | Elsewhere |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resume with `resumeFromRunId`, same script and arguments, same session | yes | yes | `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/agents.md`, "Resuming a Workflow run" |
| Finished agents keep results; an unfinished one runs from its start | yes | yes | `agents.md` |
| The journal's path and lines | yes | no ("each run's journal" survives) | `agents.md`, "The journal" |
| Longest unchanged prefix in call order; a changed prompt is a new key; a copy that changes only what follows the prefix runs the changed call live | yes | no | `agents.md`, "Matching the launched run exactly" |
| A changed script: resume from a copy as launched (`git show`; the harness's kept copy) | yes (`git show`) | no | `agents.md` (both ways) |
| Short hash misses from the first call; call order can differ; wrap `agent()` | yes | no | `agents.md` |
| A killed agent's leftovers: name them or stash and move aside | yes | no | `agents.md:73`; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5b/RECORD.md`, "A relaunched gather" |
| Background shell scripts the workers started survive | yes | yes | `agents.md` (not stated); FACTS 201; `reviews/batch-13-review.md` § 4 (the precedent of a resume one minute after the stop) |

**Pointer needed for a reader of the new entry?** Yes. The new entry says "the launch's script and arguments byte for byte" and points to `agents.md`; without that part a reader concludes that the edited script forbids a resume (and relaunches or reverts the edit), and knows nothing of the journal's form, the cached-prefix rule, the short-hash trap or the leftovers. The old entry holds all of it but the gate's own steps.

**Wrong answers from missing information.** Relaunching from the base; reverting the script edit "so that it matches byte for byte" without knowing the prefix rule (harmless but needless, and loses the intended commit prompt); giving the base as a short hash; editing a rung's prompt "to tell it about the restart" (the rung then runs again); starting a new session; not looking for the surviving distance JVM and suite; running the gate's suites by hand and pasting a summary.

**Rubric.** Decision 2: journal read first, resume in-session with the same arguments, finished agents kept and only the gate (and commit) live, the script edit handled by the prefix rule or a copy as launched, the surviving background processes and the gate's leftovers named. 1: resume right but the script edit mishandled (reverted or feared) or the surviving processes missed. 0: a relaunch, a new session, or a changed rung prompt. # Answers, record test 6

## 6. The process stopped in the gate

### What I check on disk first (reading only, in this order)

1. **The kind of stop.** I run `grep -E 'Received signal|context cancellation|Set session mode' /tmp/env-manager.log | tail` and `uptime -s`. The cap's stop has `duration_ms` near 46,640,000, and the boot time is earlier than the stop. This matters:
   - After the cap, commands started with nohup are still alive and the disk is whole.
   - After a VM restart, every process is dead and the disk may be rolled back. The gather's commits are local until the commit stage pushes, so a rollback would lose them.
2. **The boot note.** The run ID, the launch arguments kept at launch, the base, and the armed check-ins.
3. **The run's journal** (`~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/journal.jsonl`):
   - The `launched` line. It holds the arguments byte for byte (the full base hash and `baseBuild`). I check them against the copy kept at launch.
   - A `result` line for every rung worker, every skeptic, every rung judge or repair, and the gather.
   - `gate`: a `started` line and no `result` line.
   - `review`: does it have a result? It runs beside the gate, and the scenario does not say. Also any `judge:review` or `repair:review` started without a result, and any `:attempt` label.
4. **The main tree.** I run `git log --oneline <base>..HEAD` and `git status --short`. I look for:
   - the gather's commits;
   - a review commit titled "Fold the review's corrections";
   - uncommitted edits under `explorations/` (an unfinished review's);
   - my own script edit, and whether it is committed.
5. **What still runs.** `ps -eo pid,etime,args | grep -E "ant|java|fortress" | grep -v grep`, then `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd` for each process. I expect the distance stage's bash wrapper and its `DistanceMulti` JVM, and probably the suite the gate was in (`ant testFast` or `ant testSystem`, which its role starts with nohup), all in `/home/user/fortress`.
6. **The gate's logs.** `ls -lt tmp/gate-batch-14 tmp/gate-batch-14/out`, and the `EXIT=` lines of `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `distance.txt`. Also whether step 3's `ladder/root/ladder-caches` and `ladder/root/pristine` exist, and what is in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`.
7. **The script as launched.** The launch commit is not the base:
   - The base is fixed at step 1 of the manual's "Before the launch". The batch's manifest block is spliced and committed at step 4, after the base. So `<base>:<path>` holds batch 13's block.
   - The launch commit is the splice commit: the last commit that touches `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` before the time on the journal's `launched` line (`git log --format='%h %ci %s' -- <script>`).
   - I write `git show <launch commit>:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` to the scratchpad. I check that it says `const BATCH = '14'`, and that its diff with the current file is my one sentence in `commitRole` and nothing else.

### What the stopped gate left behind, that the resumed one meets

The resumed gate does not get its recovery text. `callAgent` puts `retryHead(..., recoverGate())` at the head of the prompt only on attempt 2, after `agent()` returned nothing. A resume issues the same attempt-1 call under the same key. That call has no result, so it runs live from its start, with the launch prompt, which assumes a fresh start. That prompt would meet the following:

- **The distance stage, still running.** A nohup command survives the cap. The gate's step 2 starts a second one "at once", with:
  - the same out-file, `out/distance.txt`;
  - the same log, `distance.txt`, truncated, with two writers;
  - the same scratch folder, whose caches the first run deletes when it ends.

  That makes two `-Xmx4g` JVMs beside four-thread suites, on 15 GB of memory with no swap. The `distance.txt` that lands would be wrong, or the stage would die.
- **A suite that may still be running.**
  - Step 2's `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS` deletes the suite's results while it runs.
  - `ant compileAll` writes `ProjectFortress/build` under the running suite and the distance JVM.
  - A second suite beside the first deletes the `test-caches` that the first one uses. Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts, and only one suite may run in a tree at a time.

  The likely result is a red gate with no real cause, then a gate judge and a repair spent on it.
- **Step 3's ladder copies, already in place.** `cp -a default_repository/caches .../ladder-caches` onto a directory that already exists puts a new copy inside it. The old copy stays where the ladder reads it, and the disk fills faster.
- **Partial files.** `testFast.txt` or `testSystem.txt`, `out/distance.txt`, `TEST-RESULTS`, and what is left in `test-caches` and `test-tmp`.
- **The main tree.** The gather's commits, perhaps the review's corrections commit and an unfinished review's uncommitted edits, and my script edit if it is not committed.

### How I bring the run back, and with what

I resume the run and never relaunch it:

    Workflow({scriptPath: <the copy>, args: <the launched line's args, byte for byte>, resumeFromRunId: '<run id>'})

What the copy holds, and what I do with the leftovers, depends on one fact in the journal: whether the review returned. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of calls, in call order. The script issues the gate's call (line 1952) before the review's (line 1954).

**If the review returned** (the likely case: it builds nothing, and the gate was still in its suites):

- The copy stays byte for byte as launched. If I changed the gate's prompt, every later key would change, and the finished review would run again from its start. Its launch prompt does not know about its own corrections commit, so its `headBefore` and `pathsOutsideExplorations` would miss them. The script uses those to decide whether the gate runs again, so that decision would go wrong.

Fortress revival · 2026-08-19 to 10-10

The revival so far

Written 2026-10-08, updated 2026-10-13, for the curator. Dates without a year are 2026, times UTC. Each part ends with its sources.

Six parts

  1. The start and the exploring era
  2. The unsealed tree and the batches
  3. How the record grew
  4. Since 10-04: the skills and the process
  5. What the revival changed in Fortress
  6. The original Fortress and the revival's resolutions

Words used throughout:

team
Sun Labs designers of Fortress. Their last commit is a874948ac (2012-08-31).
walk
Interpreter. It runs a program with no static types.
compiled path
Path that compiles a program to JVM bytecode and runs it: fortress compile, then fortress run.
checker
Static type checker. It runs on the compiled path only.
library
Fortress code that every program loads. There were two. The interpreter's is the one library. The compiler's own smaller one is the prelude.
switch-over
Point at which the compiled path moves onto the one library and the prelude is deleted. It comes when the checker accepts the one library.
gap ledger
File with one numbered row for each known gap or defect.

1The start and the exploring era (08-19 to 09-16)

The 2012 tree builds and runs again

  • 08-18 and 08-19: the tree built on JDK 8, and the team's tests ran: about 1.4K in testFast, 382 in testSystem.

2The unsealed tree and the batches (09-17 to 10-10)

How a batch works. A batch is one run of a workflow script.

  • A rung is one piece of work, done by a worker in its own checkout of the tree.
  • A skeptic checks each rung. Up to batch 10, if it refused, a judge ruled, a repair agent fixed, and a second skeptic checked. Since batch 11 the skeptic fixes what it finds, and a judge rules only on a contested fix.
  • The gather folds each rung's notes into the record. A merged-diff review reads the combined change.
  • The gate is the full check before landing: the build, both suites, compiled atomic programs at four threads, the ladder (below), and the checker's error counts. To land is to commit to main and push.
  • After each batch, one reviewer checks it against the decisions and the designers' intent.

The first climbs (09-17 to 09-20). The ladder is 410 of the team's test programs pushed through the compiled path. On the sealed tree 59 passed.

  • The ladder climb (09-17): eight rungs added names to the prelude and compiled a top-level var. 81 passed. A review found one rung against the specification and one departing from it without a reason.

  • The flat number tower (09-24). The checker keeps the team's rule that no type extends two instantiations of one generic trait. The one library's nested number types broke it, so they became siblings that convert by declared coercions, as in the prelude. Walk learned coercion in batch 4; the library was flattened in batch 6.   • Sizes at run time (09-24). A size parameter (nat) gets the run-time descriptor a type argument has. Since batch 5, a sized program compiles and runs.
