## 2. Q1: a body at narrower parameter types defines an inherited abstract method

### 2.1 What landed

`Constructor.checkForDef` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java:423-453`) refuses an object, or an object expression, without static parameters that inherits a declaration without a body, unless `definedBelow` (`:466-484`) finds, among what the object's traits provide, one declaration with a body of the same name and self position whose parameter types are each a subtype, equality included, of the abstract declaration's. One such body is enough: nothing asks that the bodies together cover the abstract declaration's parameter types. A body whose parameter types walk cannot read counts too (`:480-482`). The residue is gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXAbstractMethodPartlyDefinedWalk.fss` (row 666: `tag(self, x: ZZ32) = 1` under the abstract `tag(self, x: Number)` loads). The record states it so (FACTS, "Walk refuses at load an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, ..."; PLAN, "Pavol's answers", item 51, and `PLAN.md:116`).

### 2.2 The chapter's letter

- A trait inherits the method declarations its immediate supertraits provide, "except those method declarations that are overridden ... or whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter) is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration that occurs in the trait declaration" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:521-527`).
- "An abstract method declaration declares an abstract method; any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the method" (`:570-572`; the Working Draft of February 2011 has the same words, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex:511`, and so does the 1.0 release).

Read literally, as the worker read it (`REPORT.md:121-128`, section 5): an object whose own declarations are at narrower types has none with the abstract declaration's parameter type, so it inherits the abstract declaration and must define it; a narrower body, alone or with others, does not. That refuses the landed allowance and the coverage shape alike.

The chapter is not of one mind, though. Its own sentence on functional methods says "An abstract function declaration ... can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations" (`:558-560`), and the rule for abstract function declarations, as the revival revised it under the type group's reading of a `comprises` clause, asks for coverage: "the argument types of the concrete declarations for f must together cover T", "a definition for every type listed in the comprises clause of Molecule, or definitions that together cover those types, or it is a static error" (`Specification/basic/functions.tex:386-395`, `:431-434`, the callouts `revival-covering` at `:396-400` and `:435-444`). The Meet Rule has its covering case in the same words (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:312-336`). Only the sentence at `traits.tex:570-572` is older than that reading.

### 2.3 The team's later word

- **The compiled checker, Guy Steele, May 2012.** `AbstractMethodChecker.checkObjectDeclaration` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala:81-122`, the comment "GLS 5/30/12" at `:112`): "For each abstract method, check to see whether it is covered by one or more concrete definitions" (`:96`). It takes the concrete declarations of the name and self position whose domains are below the abstract one's, joins their domains into a union, and refuses the object unless the abstract domain is a subtype of that union. A lone narrower body fails it; narrower bodies that together cover pass it.
- **His next commit, 59fdeff62, 2012-06-06**: `TypeAnalyzer` reads a `comprises` clause when it asks whether a closed trait is below a union, "This should improve the behavior of 'covers' checks in AbstractMethodChecker" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:154-158`). So the checker's coverage reads `comprises` clauses, on purpose, since June 2012. The worker measured it: `CoverAbstractProbe`, the shape of `trait D comprises { P, Q }` with abstract `f(self, other: D)` and `P` declaring `f` over `P` and over `Q`, type checks (exit 0), and `PartAbstractProbe`, row 666's program, is refused, "Domain Number is not a subtype of ZZ32" (`REPORT.md:147-148`).
- **Welterweight Fortress, 2012.** The Covered judgement: "The notion of 'covering' is a generalization of the notion of 'overriding,' because an abstract function with an argument that is a trait type with a comprises clause is considered to be covered if it is implemented for all the types comprised"; "the domain type of an abstract function ... must be a subtype of the union of the domains of the concrete definitions"; and "the same rules are used to check methods as well as functions, and for methods, the type of the trait or object within which the method is declared is not considered" (`Papers/Welterweight/static.tick:27-47`; the rule, `Papers/Welterweight/fig-covered.tick:9-13`).
- **The internal FAQ**: "An abstract method can be implemented by concrete methods whose return types are subtypes of the abstract method" (`Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex:159-162`), several concrete methods for one abstract one.
- **The later restart** says nothing: its Types, traits, declarations, objects and overloading chapters hold neither "abstract" nor "override" (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/*.tick`).
- **The team's walk** never made the check: its `checkForDef` returned for every `FnDecl`, body or not (`Constructor.java:399-404` at `a874948ac`), which is row 649.

By the record's weighing, the checker's rule and Welterweight's are the type group's late position, written by the team member who wrote the chapter; they outweigh the sentence at `traits.tex:570-572`.

### 2.4 The team's library and tests

- `Library/Pairs.fss:78-99`: `trait RunRanges comprises { SingleRange, RangeSet }` with abstract `opr BOXPLUS(self, x: RunRanges)`; `SingleRange` defines `BOXPLUS` over `SingleRange` and over `RangeSet`, and `RangeSet` likewise. The coverage shape, in the team's library. # Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it: "It builds P-48."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: the fact as it stands now; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; the test that gates it, or its source; the decision it builds, by number; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; what it means for the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check with one bounded `grep` that the cited report section holds what the entry left out.
4. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. Run it on FACTS before each batch launches, since the batch's workers read it.

- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

## INDEX and the gap ledger

- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`). Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the
record file and its history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root

- **The team's own example.** `Pairs` in the team's library declares `trait RunRanges comprises { SingleRange, RangeSet }`, with an abstract `BOXPLUS(self, x: RunRanges)`.
  - Each of the two objects defines `BOXPLUS` twice: once for `x: SingleRange` and once for `x: RangeSet`.
  - Neither body takes `RunRanges` itself, but together they cover it.
  - The team's test `FileConversion` has the same shape.
- **The old wording.** The specification's traits chapter says "any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the method". Read literally, that means a body at the same parameter type.
- **The team's later word.** Steele's compiled checker of May 2012 checks coverage: the bodies together must cover the abstract method's parameter types. His next commit, in June 2012, made that check read `comprises` clauses. Welterweight's rule says the same. The revised specification already uses coverage for abstract functions.
- **What walk does today.** It accepts any single narrower body, which is looser than both readings. That's a stopgap from batch 12.

Not on its own, because the two measures are linked.

- **The distance (85)** counts every error the compiled checker finds in the interpreter's library. 79 of the 85 are in the library's main code file.
- **The count (1)** looks at the same library but stops at the first error in that file. In batch 13 that first error was `isLeftZero`. Once that was fixed, the first error became `body(i)` in `__bigOperator`, a parameter with no type written. That's the switch you remember.

So the count is 0 only once that file has no errors at all, which means the distance there is 0 too. The count is the distance seen through a keyhole: getting it to 0 is the same job as getting the distance to 0, which is the rest of this phase.

It will also look worse before it gets better:

- Batch 14 types `body(i)`, but the count stays 1. The checker then runs into the next stop, a crash in `Array3`'s `plane` (row 680), which counts as one error.
- Once that crash is fixed, the count stops stopping early. It jumps to the file's real errors, dozens at that point. That isn't a regression; it's the true number showing.
- That crash also hides `Array3`'s body from the distance. So the distance is a floor: about 54 after batch 14, plus whatever is behind it.

The distance is the number to drive down, and the count just tells us where the checker stops first.

Noted: batch 14 launches once the check of the fold comes back clean.

No, Fable didn't review this one. The manual has a Fable reviewer check each batch plan, and batches 9 to 13 had one. This time an Opus reviewer did it. That follows your word from last night, "Opus checks instead" of Fable reviews, and it saves Fable's weekly budget. The Opus review found real problems and fixed them, for example the four declarations the self-type rule would refuse. If you'd still like a Fable pass before launch, it costs about 1M Fable tokens and an hour.

The process from here:

1. **The check finishes.** The Opus reviewer re-checks the new walk fix and the folded answers against the code.
2. **Before the launch, done by me:**
   - write the batch's settings into the workflow script and commit them;
   - build the starting code once, in its own copy of the repository, in about 3 minutes;
   - prove one copy can be cloned from that build, and that the old code runs from it;
   - check the disk;
   - set reminders 45 minutes apart, so the session survives a forced stop.
3. **The run, about 6 hours:**
   - Each of the five fixes gets its own worker in its own copy of the repository, and writes a failing test first.
   - A checker reviews each fix and repairs what it finds. A judge rules only if the checker contests a repair.
   - Then the fixes are merged. A review of the merged diff runs alongside the full test gate, which also measures the count and the distance.
   - Then the commit.
4. **After it lands:**
   - The record's facts are updated.
   - The skill writer updates the fortress-repo skill's list of what the revival changed.
   - An Opus reviewer checks the landed changes against your decisions.
   - I bring you the result and the review list.

You'll hear from me when it lands or if it stops. While it runs, I stay quiet.

Yes. Each fix's brief ends with a list of keys, each with one line on why it's there. A key is a record entry's number (such as `P-146`), a gap-ledger row, a specification section, a section of a note, or a span of code. The worker's first step runs the extract script over all the keys, and the script prints each one in order. Before the batch was drafted, the script checked that every key resolves to exactly one place: all of them do.

Against the consolidated record, measured just now:

- **The same 41 record entries print 24K bytes now, against 69K before last night's consolidation.** That's 65% smaller.
- **But record entries are a small part of each briefing.** The five briefings print 358K bytes in all, about 25K to 30K tokens per fix. Most of that is specification sections, judgements and notes. So the consolidation shrinks this batch's briefings by about 11%.
- **The library fix's briefing is the smallest at 31K bytes.** The other four are 76K to 86K each.

The next saving in the briefings would be the notes and judgements they quote whole, not the record.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/fortress-repo

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the run time), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, run your test on both paths. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
5. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
6. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over comes when the checker accepts the interpreter's library.

### The compiled run time

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss":12:1~156:2 ...`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A `value` object has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`.

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself, such as `SUM`'s, stays open, and every value passes it. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch: logs, captured output, probe programs. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. Each agent's transcript keeps how the work was done (`references/committing.md`).
- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).

## The parts

Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.

The parts, in the order that work meets them:

- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the run time, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands: `references/compiler.md`
- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
- What the revival changed in the team's Fortress, each change with its contradiction and reason; load it when a team source, an old note or your training disagrees with this skill: `references/revival-changes.md`
- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.

A task usually needs several parts, and every task needs `records.md`, for its queries and its report. For example, a fix of walk needs `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$LineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$ToString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Eq")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Index")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Cmp")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$CICmp")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Substr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$IndexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## The library order

The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.

Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:

- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.

Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:

    cd ProjectFortress
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s

Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.

- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.

  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start.       cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Check-ins, for the coordinating session

Check-ins keep the session busy across a long run. Each wake falls inside the main session's one-hour prompt cache, so it reads the cache instead of writing the whole context again. Each turn's end also runs the transcript backup (`hooks.md`).

- Arm all the check-ins of a series in one turn, 45 minutes apart. Use no cron trigger, whose shortest interval is an hour. Do not chain reminders, each check-in arming the next one.
- The scheduler refuses more than about ten trigger creations a minute ("Trigger creation rate limit reached"). If it refuses one, arm the rest a minute later.
- A series ends with its last check-in. If the run outlasts it, have the last check-in arm a whole new series.
- Add one check-in a few minutes after the cap's next stop, 12 h 58 min after the last start. In its message, tell the session to resume what the stop killed.
- After a stop, or when you relaunch a run, delete or re-arm the reminders to fit the run.
- An interrupt of any turn, one that a check-in started included, kills the run's agents. If the curator means to stop the session while agents run, ask them to wait until the turn has ended and about 10 s more, for the backup's pass.

content.text:
The coordinator never edits a skill, so I didn't write it. It wasn't on the record before either. Here's how it got there:

1. **17:16 UTC on 13 October (19:16 your time).** You told me there'd be no Fable adversarial reviews that night, Opus checks instead, and not to take Fable's ideas as gospel. That message went on the held list as point 7.
2. **19:22 UTC that night (21:22 yours).** The skill writer drafted the new coordinator skill from scratch. Its sources file cites exactly that held point for this line. The writer turned a one-night instruction about the record consolidation into a standing rule: "Fable reviews tend to keep everything as it was. For a check, an Opus worker is enough." That synthesis is the writer's, not your words.
3. **19:46 UTC.** The fixes after the cold read only reworded it.
4. **Later that night.** I closed point 7 on the held list as "held by the skill", so nobody checked the rule's scope against your words.
5. **Last night, before batch 14.** I applied the standing rule to the batch plan's review. That's how the Fable review nearly got skipped.

So it was overreach twice: the writer widened your instruction, and I acted on the widened version.

Holding it for the skill fine-tuning. I'll write it onto the held list once the batch lands, because the batch's commit step needs the main tree untouched until then.

# Rewriting a skill

The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, which every agent is.

**writer**
: Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, with its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`.

**cold read**
: Reading of a rewritten part by a worker given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`). It flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, and each undefined term.

## The method

1. Draft the outline first, with a home for every rule that moves.
2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them.
4. Publish the part as a page. The curator reads it whole.
5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. Ask the curator only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter.

- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, and keep the review page in step.
- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.
- After each batch's landing, have the writer update `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md`: what the revival changed in the language, each change with its contradiction and its reason. Its `SKILL.md` keeps only what does not change from batch to batch.

## The coordinator skill

This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:

- Guide lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to the curator in each situation. Write no set of many small rules that may contradict each other.
- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.
- Keep a rule if the failure that it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing.
- Write the list of kept rules into the writer's task. The writer writes from scratch, without reading the old skill. A worker then checks the draft against that list, and the cold read follows.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts or resumes the skill writer: a headless Claude session that edits the
# project skills. A headless session writes its prompt cache with the one-hour
# life, where an Agent-tool subagent gets five minutes, so a writer resumed
# within the hour reads its context from the cache.
#
# Usage:
#   skill-writer.sh new <task-file>     a fresh writer: the standing brief
#                                       (../skill-writer-brief.md), then the task
#   skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>  the task, sent to the current writer
#
# The session id and each task's JSON output are kept under the repository's
# tmp/skill-writer/, which is ignored. The script prints the writer's report,
# its session id and the tokens the task wrote to the cache.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.." && pwd)
state="$repo/tmp/skill-writer"
mkdir -p "$state"
mode=${1:?new or resume}
task=$(cd "$(dirname "${2:?task file}")" && pwd)/$(basename "$2")
tools=(Read Edit Write Glob Grep
       "Bash(git add:*)" "Bash(git commit:*)" "Bash(git diff:*)" "Bash(git log:*)"
       "Bash(git status:*)" "Bash(git show:*)" "Bash(git grep:*)" "Bash(wc:*)"
       "Bash(explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh:*)"
       "Bash(python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py:*)")

You are an Opus worker in the Fortress revival repository (`/home/user/fortress`, branch `main`). You write one page for the curator: the final report on climb batch 14, after its landing, its review and the record's update. He reads on an iPhone, often with iOS Speak reading aloud at a fast rate. You run no Fortress program and read no session transcripts. Load the `fortress-repo` skill, and the `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md` (its sections "Talking to the curator" and "Pages").

## Sources

- The batch record `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-14.md` (section 1 for the words and what each fix is), the gather's record `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-14/RECORD.md`, the gate `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-14/gate/`, the landing commit `7c2c7cd4b`'s message, and the post-batch review `explorations/reviews/batch-14-review.md` (conformance, the distance, the cost by role against batches 11 to 13, the practice, the items for the curator).
- PLAN (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`): phase 3's items for batch 14 and batch 15, and "Climb batch 14, listed for his review".
- What happened to the record after the landing: `git log --oneline 7c2c7cd4b..HEAD` (the FACTS pass, the POSITIONS pass, the skill writer's commits, the routing).

## The page

Title "Batch 14 Landed". Six sections, each short, in plain short sentences with contractions; lists, not tables; numbers as K or M; every term defined where first used; no handles from the record (no "F-53", "P-146", "rung S", "item 51"): name things by what they are.

1. **The answer.** Landed or not, the gate, the distance and the count, the cost, in four or five lines.
2. **What changed in Fortress.** The five fixes, each in two or three sentences: what a Fortress programmer or the checker now does differently, with a one-line example where it helps.
3. **The cost.** Tokens written, by role, against batches 11, 12 and 13, from the review's figures; per fix; why it fell (no judge, no refusal cycles, the parts that ran shorter). The curator asked whether the process changes paid off: answer that from the figures, plainly, with what one batch can and cannot show.
4. **How the work was done.** Test first (each checker confirmed it from the transcripts), the checkers' fixes and that none was contested, the briefing's use, the two tool defects the batch showed and their fixes (the count stage's stated time, the measuring script's build count).
5. **For your review.** The review's items for the curator, sorted by his rule of 00:12 UTC today, which the boot note states (`explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, "How forks reach him"): an item that the record's principles settle (the team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, the peers) is listed with what landed and the coordinator's call, one line each, and needs nothing from him; an item that touches the goal (microGPT, its speed, its readability), would reverse one of his decisions, or where the principles split, or that a rule of his reserves for him (an extension of the library is his to judge, `process-engineering/library-extension-rule-archaeology.md` §5 point 4), is named as one for him, with a two-sentence primer in plain words and a Fortress example, and its default. Say once that nothing here holds the work. Where you cannot tell which kind an item is from its evidence, say so and put it with his.
6. **Next.** Batch 15's candidates as PLAN gives them, with what each waits on, and the distance they could reach.

Each section's references (commits, files as GitHub URLs `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`) at its bottom, numbered, outside what its Select button selects.

href="https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/commit/bc9208255">bc9208255. INDEX and the review queue: 4c3b2e42a.

For your review

These are the items the batch and its review left for you, sorted by your rule of 00:12 UTC today (02:12 yours). A fork that the record's principles settle, meaning the team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, or the peers, the coordinator decides and lists. A fork on the goal, one that would reverse a decision of yours, one where the principles split, or one that a rule of yours reserves comes to you. Nothing here holds the work. Each default is what landed, or what's in place now.

For you

The count's one error. Every reduction and comprehension runs through the library function __bigOperator, whose local body(i) gives i no type, and the checker refuses that, as you answered. Writing body(i: I) makes walk refuse list and map comprehensions, because walk gives I the empty type when nothing fixes it. Example: xs = <| 2 k | k <- 0#3 |> prints <|0, 2, 4|> today, and with the type written it stops with “body param 1 (i:BOTTOM) got arg 4”. Default: the line stays untyped, and the count stays 1. It's yours because the two ways are your open question on walk's plain-bounded parameters, or an untyped fn (i) => ... that goes against your answer.

numerator on each integer type, an extension of the library. numerator gives a number's numerator as a ZZ, the unbounded integer, and for an integer it's the integer itself. The checker refused the default body in the trait Integral, so the fix removed it and declared numerator(self): ZZ on ZZ32, ZZ64, NN32 and NN64: four new api lines, the declarations in the interface files, copied from ZZ's own. Example: numerator(7), with 7 a ZZ32, still answers the ZZ 7. Default: as landed. It's yours by your library rule: you judge each extension, shown the line it copies.

Team declarations changed in Random and QuickCheck. Under your coverage answer, walk refuses an object whose bodies don't cover an inherited abstract method, and three library places relied on the old allowance. The fix gave each a body copied from a line of its own file: the seeded distribution wrapper passes seedSize and reseed to the generator it wraps, Mersenne Twister's setup takes perturbed at the abstract declaration's type, Generator[\ZZ32\], and QuickCheck's any-value generator gets Gen's default perturb. Example: perturb(obj: Any, g) = g, where before a call outside its one narrower body stopped walk with “has neither body nor def”. Default: as landed. It's yours because the review counts these api lines as extensions, and I can't tell from the evidence whether they're plain repairs that the library's own text settles.

Walk and a call written as another call's argument. Walk has no static types, so it doesn't give an argument the expected type that the checker now gives it. With mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\], takesBox64(mk()) runs compiled but stops under walk, and where another declaration accepts Any, walk runs that one, a different answer from the compiled program. Example: under walk, takesBox64(mk()) stops with “got arg BoxT[\Any\]”. Default: walk unchanged, the gap marked by an expected failure. It's yours because the record leaves to you whether and where walk should take an argument's static arguments from the declaration around it, and I can't tell whether the principles settle that.

Walk's coverage search when it can't finish. To check coverage, walk splits each parameter type into the cases its comprises list names, up to a limit, and past the limit it now accepts the object, as another of walk's checks does, while the compiled checker refuses it. Your coverage answer makes walk agree with the checker, so the two pull different ways, and no program in the suites, the 62 demos or the specification's examples reaches the limit. Example: a method of five parameters, each of a type with six cases, makes about 7.8K combinations, and walk loads the object that the checker refuses. Default: walk accepts, and an expected failure marks the gap. It's yours because the principles split.

IntMap's disjoint join with a one-entry map. UPLUS joins two maps that mustn't share a key, and its comment promises a KeyOverlap error when they do. A one-entry map on the left throws, but on the right the join quietly keeps the many-entry map's value, where the library's own addNew would throw. Example: {0 |-> 0, 1 |-> 1, 2 |-> 2} UPLUS {1 |-> 9} answers the three-entry map unchanged, while the other order throws. Default: today's value, pinned by a test. It's yours because the team's code and its comment disagree, and the record leaves the repair to your word.

The team's trips demo, refused by the self-type rule. The demo declares object generator(...) extends StandardTotalOrder[\trip\], but a generator isn't a trip, so the checker now refuses it, while walk still runs the demo and no gated test reads it. A one-line edit to StandardTotalOrder[\generator\] would match the order its own CMP defines. Default: the demo stays as it is. It's yours because an edit goes against your word on the demos: leave them, and make them run later.

Settled, nothing needed from you

The mixin reading of the self-type rule. A trait's parameter, bounded by a self-typed trait that it extends at that parameter, counts as its self parameter, as Scala reads a self-type annotation, so the team's 2009 Containment mixins check clean. That reads the library as the team wrote it. The coordinator's call: as built.

Three readings in the self-type text. A comprises list of only ... counts as none, the extender check compares a trait's self type as Scala's conformance rule does, and the text names the new term “self-type parameter”. Nothing measured moves. The call: as built.

The retry reaches a reduction's big operator. s: ZZ32 = BIG LAST[j <- lo#n] (3 j) now compiles, while one whose parameter's bound names itself, like SUM's, is still refused. Your answer's words cover it. The call: as built.

The retry's three small choices. A generic call around the retried argument is fixed from its other arguments and its own expected type, a tie is refused with today's message, and a call that writes its own static arguments is retried too. Your answer's definition settles them. The call: as built.

A compiled program's answer changed, and the inference chapter gained a paragraph. mk() OPLUS mk() OPLUS mk() now runs the three-operand declaration, not the two-operand one, as the specification's text on chained operators says, and the paragraph states your answer. The call: as built.

No retry for a call without static arguments of its own. takesBox64(p(mk())), with p overloaded but not generic, stays refused, as your answer's words limit it. The call: as your answer says.

A negative exponent in a size, for your sight. Walk now refuses it, and the compiled path computes none; the specification is silent. The call: as built.

A gap row for walk's refusal of the typed body(i). The gap ledger is the record's list of known gaps, one row each. Walk's refusal got its own row, beside your open question that covers the same case, rather than being folded into it. The call: the row as filed.

A suspected type slip in Random's two distribution wrappers. No stage checks Random, so it isn't measured. The call: no row unti Shell cwd was reset to /home/user/fortress

- cloud-container: How the cloud platform this repository is worked on behaves, apart from Claude Code and the repository: the machine (4 CPUs, about 15 GB of memory, no swap, timings that differ between sessions), the disk allowance and why df misleads, a disk full with no space left on device and what to delete, the network proxy and its blocked hosts (web.archive.org, labs.oracle.com), the platform's stop of the session's process about every 13 hours, idle stops and VM restarts, a VM restart that rolls the disk back, the weekly usage limit stopping a run, send_later check-ins that keep the session busy across a stop, the transcript backup and its blind spots, reading another session's transcript, the platform's git-check Stop hook, and a lost container: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, recovering the work. Load it when the disk fills or df looks wrong, when a host cannot be reached, after the session's process was stopped or the VM restarted, when commits are missing after a restart, before arming check-ins for a long wait, when the backup fails to push, and when a container is lost or a session must go on in another.

Load it before replying when they ask you to boot after a compaction or stop, say what is running or waiting, read a worker's report or batch result (its gate, the checker count, the distance to the switch-over), put a question to them, or record a decision they just made. Not for workers, build/test work (fortress-repo), container or hook faults (cloud-container), or generic multi-agent or ADR questions.

The rule is the team's later word (POPL 2019). He ranks the team's later work above his own reading. It sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). MicroGPT's types are concrete, so it is untouched. The library keeps the team's unbounded declarations. Still to build: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static return type (row 538, PLAN phase 5).
- F-141 **Under `walk`, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes takes its declared bound, and a lone one with no narrowest candidate its bound.** It builds P-48. Its departures by the rung's decisions: an F-bounded parameter stays open (F-143); a big operator's plain-bounded ones keep `BottomType` (D2); one that only a fixed parameter's bound mentions takes the arguments' type (D3, row 592); a lone one whose bound mentions a static parameter keeps the arguments' narrowest common supertype (D5). Its departures as defects, each with an expected failure: several bounds that walk cannot meet (row 591); a bound only from above that mentions a static parameter (row 612); an untyped function expression's result (row 587); a generic passed over at dispatch when its arguments have several minimal common supertypes (row 589), whose repair changes which declaration runs. Gated by `tests/Infer*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-instance/REPORT.md` section 2.
- F-94 **The compiled checker checks the array family under the bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`, but fails calls through a parameter so bounded.** It refuses a call whose argument's type holds the caller's parameter (row 686), as at the library's `squaredNorm(me)`. It crashes on a call whose argument is the parameter, or that converts a numeral beside it (rows 689, 687). Writing the static argument avoids all three. It refuses a valid overloading beside such a declaration (row 690). A memo on the trait table keeps the count stage within its 900-second limit (row 688). Gated by `OverloadTwoBoundsClosed*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-array-bound/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 9.
- F-220 **Under walk, `__bigOperator`'s local `body` cannot be typed `I`, since an unwritten list or map comprehension gives `I` the type `BottomType`; so the checker count's one error stays at the untyped `body(i)`.** Walk keeps a big operator's plain-bounded parameter at `BottomType` (F-141, D2). Typing `body(i)` waits on review-queue item 17 (PLAN item 53). An untyped function expression in `body`'s place runs under walk; the checker's verdict on it is not measured. No gated test can show the refusal: row 703 gives the program and its output. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-followups/REPORT.md` section 2.

  # Walk's plain-bounded big-operator parameter: the ways to P-48, measured
  
  ## 1. The answer
  
  | way | kind | interpreter tests (604) | spec examples (130) | rows 645 / 646 / 662 | `body(i: I)` (row 703) |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | base: `BottomType` (D2) | today | all green | all green | open / open / open | refused |
  | 2. the comprehension's collection built from its elements, with the bound | library + walk | 21 red | all green | open / open / open | not measured |
  | 4. the declared bound (P-48 as written) | walk | 7 red | 1 red | open / open / open | not measured |
  | 5. the open type, as F-143 gives an F-bounded one | walk | all green | all green | open / open / open | runs |
  | 6. the desugaring by the elements' type | walk + library | 2 changed, both promotions | all green | open / fixed / fixed | runs |
  | 6 + 7. and the call's static return type where walk has one | walk + library | 3 changed, all promotions | all green | fixed / fixed / fixed | runs |
  
  The way to brief is 6 + 7 (`patches/wayDE-elements-expected-body.patch`). It keeps every checked value. A clause form with no element and no declared type takes the bound, as P-48 says. A declared type comes first, as P-48's "constrained by the call's static return type" says. Otherwise the instance is the join of the elements' run-time types, which stands in for the specification's desugaring by the type `N` of the expression. It promotes three expected failures (rows 645, 646 and 662) and lets `__bigOperator` type `body(i: I)` in the same rung. microGPT's quick pair passes 7 of 7 twice.
  
  Its one reading to confirm (section 9, question 1): P-48 rules out "the value's type alone" for a parameter that the arguments do not fix. Way 6 counts a clause form's parameter as fixed by its elements, the run-time stand-in for the type `N` with which the specification's desugaring writes it. Way 5 is the closest alternative. It changes no verdict at all, and `body(i: I)` lands with it too. But its instance is the open type, a kind of `BottomType`, and it leaves rows 645, 646 and 662 and the unwritten `BIG CONCAT` as they are.
  
  ## 2. The question and the record
  
  - P-48: the instance of a type parameter that the arguments do not fix is the intersection of its upper bounds, constrained by the call's static return type, never `Bottom`.
  - F-141: under walk such a parameter takes its declared bound, with these departures:
    - D2: a big operator's plain-bounded parameters keep `BottomType`, at `EvaluatorBase.java:170`, `boolean bounds = bounded && !bigOperator(appliedThing);`;
    - F-143: an F-bounded parameter stays open.
  - F-220 and row 703: because of D2, `__bigOperator`'s local `body(i)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1314`) cannot be typed `I`.
  - Review-queue item 17, PLAN item 53 and rows 645 and 662: giving the bound broke six tests at rung W's base (`compile-ladder/rung-walk-instance/REPORT.md` section 6.1).
  
  The mechanism is as follows:
  - The desugarer passes the big operator with only the static arguments that the program writes: `__bigOperator(BIG OP(), fn (r, u) => ...)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:404-408`).
  - `__bigOperator` takes `o.reduction` before any element exists (`FortressLibrary.fss:1312-1316`).
  - The library's comprehensions are built by the team's covariant collections (`Library/CovariantCollection.fss:136-146`). The reduction's identity is `Empty[\T\]`, and the result is lifted to `T` by `upward(Empty[\T\], xs)`.
  - At `T = BottomType` that lift does nothing, so the result is built at the join of the elements' run-time types. At the bound it is built at the bound.
  
  The specification desugars a clause form with the type of the expression. `<| e | gs |>` of type `List[\E\]` uses `BIG <|[\E\]|>`, and `SUM[gs] e` of type `N` uses `SUM[\N\]` (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex`, figure `generatedExpressions`, `:154-197`). So in the specification the desugaring fixes the parameter, and P-48's bound applies to it only where walk lacks that type.

  1. **Write the static argument** (the library's and the programs' own way; answer 7's rule; the revival box in `Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:38-44`). Under way 4, each of the eight changed sites needs one written argument:

     - `CVReduction.join` passes an `AnyEmpty` operand over;

  4. **The declared bound, P-48 as written**: D2 lifted, one line (`patches/wayA-bound.patch`). Measured: 7 interpreter tests and 1 specification example red (section 5).
  5. **The open type, as F-143 gives an F-bounded parameter**: a big operator's unfixed plain-bounded parameter becomes `BottomType.OPEN` (`patches/wayB-open.patch`, 11 lines in `instanceOf`). Measured: no verdict changes. The empty list comprehension prints `ArrayList[\OPEN\]` where the base prints `ArrayList[\BOTTOM\]`. `BIG CONCAT` unwritten still stops, 'lift param 1 (r:List[\OPEN\])'. Rows 645, 646 and 662 are unchanged.
  6. **The desugaring by the elements' type** (`patches/wayD-elements.patch`), the run-time stand-in for `N`:
     - D2 is lifted.
     - `Evaluator.for_RewriteFnApp` recognises `__bigOperator(BIG OP, clauses)` with no written static argument. It runs the clauses once through a new library reduction (`__ElemsReduction`, in `FortressLibrary.fss` after `__bigOperator`). That reduction collects the elements in order, typed at their join by the same generic inference that `APPCOV` uses.
     - It then evaluates the big operator with that join as a hint. `inferWithCoercionOrFail` unifies the hint with the first static argument of the operator's declared `Comprehension`, `BigReduction` or `BigOperator` result.
     - It then runs `__bigOperator` over the collected elements (`__replayOf`), so each body runs once.
     - With no element there is no hint, and the parameter takes its bound.
     - The per-argument-type instance caches (`OverloadedFunction.java:1414`, `:1430`; `GenericFunctionOrConstructor.java:52`, `:55`) are bypassed while a hint is set. Without that, a nullary big operator reuses its first instance: a nested comprehension printed `ArrayList[\Object\]` before the bypass and `ArrayList[\ArrayList[\Int\]\]` after it.
     - `IntMap`'s `opr BIG {|->[\Val\] }` is declared to return `IntMap[\Val\]` while its body returns a `Comprehension` (`Library/IntMap.fsi:82`, `IntMap.fss:732`). So the patch corrects its declared result, and the api imports `AnyCovColl`. Without it, `IntMap`'s comprehension took the bound, `NodeIM[\Any\]`.
  7. **The call's static return type where walk has one**, on top of 6 (`patches/wayDE-elements-expected-body.patch`, which also types `body(i: I)`). Where an unwritten clause form is the whole value of a variable declared with a type (`BuildLetEnvironments.java:80`) or of a function declared with a return type (`FunctionClosure.java:199`), that type is unified first with the operator's result type `O`. It is the second static argument of `Comprehension` and `BigOperator`, the first of `BigReduction`. The elements' join is used only where that fails. Row 510's general repair (`XXXInferExpectedTypeRungK.fss`) does not move under this way.
  8. **The specification's desugaring by the static type `N`**: the compiled path's road (row 425). Walk has no static types. Not a walk shadow.
  9. **`BottomType`**: today's D2, the base column.
